summary: This document profiles the Certificate Management Protocol, the Certificate Request Message Format, and their HTTP or CoAP transfer for simple, interoperable, automated PKI operations. It is aimed at industrial and IoT use. Only the most important operations and options are kept, to make certificate management easy on constrained devices.

plainLanguage.summary:
CMP is the protocol a device uses to ask a certificate authority for a certificate. The full protocol has many options, and two independent implementations can easily end up incompatible.

RFC 9483 is a profile of CMP. It keeps the operations a device really needs, spells out exactly how each message must be built, and pushes the harder work to the server side, so that a small device has little to implement.

subtitle: A trimmed-down profile of CMP that lets industrial and IoT devices get and renew certificates automatically.

tldr.problem: CMP and CRMF offer a very large set of features and options, and many details are left open, so a full implementation is unrealistic for constrained devices and independent implementations may not interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The profile narrows CMP down to a few mandatory operations, such as initial enrollment and certificate update, specifies exhaustively how to build each message, and allows HTTP or CoAP transfer. Heavier logic is placed in the registration authorities rather than in the devices.
tldr.outcome: A conforming end entity only has to implement a small mandatory set, while more specialized needs such as central key generation, polling and batching stay available as optional features.

today: RFC 9483 was published in November 2023 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its algorithm guidance lives in RFC 9481.

sections.title: Why a Lightweight Profile
sections.content:
CMP was standardized in 1999 and its second version, RFC 4210, with the Certificate Request Message Format of RFC 4211, was published in 2005. CMP over HTTP followed in 2012. CMP is capable and implemented in several products, but it offers a very large set of features and options, and a full implementation supporting all of them is not realistic because it would take undue effort.

Profiling is the answer: keep the strengths of the protocol, narrow the options down to what the target use case needs, and remove the ambiguities. Where there was a choice about where complexity should live, this profile puts it in the PKI management entity, where more computing resources are usually available, rather than in the end entity.

The scenarios that motivate this work are industrial and machine-to-machine ones. The profiles in Appendices D and E of RFC 4210 were built for human users and only partly cover unattended devices, and they do not address the profiling of the communication between a registration authority and a certificate authority that full back-end automation needs. Industrial systems add further challenges: network segmentation, asynchronous communication, and certification authorities that sit in a protected data centre rather than on site.
sections.plainLanguage: CMP has grown a large set of options, and a device that implements all of them would be far too heavy. This document keeps only what an automated device needs, and puts the complicated parts on the server side where there is more memory and processing power.

sections.title: The PKI Architecture
sections.content:
A device is typically equipped with a manufacturer-issued certificate, installed during production, which identifies the device for its whole life. That certificate can protect the initial enrolment of operational certificates, which are issued by the owner or operator of the device for use in protocols such as IPsec, TLS or SSH. In IEEE 802.1AR the manufacturer certificate is called an Initial Device Identifier certificate and the operational one a Locally Significant Device Identifier certificate.

Every operation in this profile follows the pull model: the end entity starts it. The end entity builds a CMP request, protects it with an asymmetric credential or with shared secret information, and sends it to a PKI management entity. That entity is usually a registration authority, which checks the request and either answers it or forwards it upstream to the next management entity, which may be a certificate authority. If a registration authority changes the header or the body of a request, or wants to show that it verified and authorised the request, it can apply protection of its own.

Figure 1 of the RFC shows the chain end entity, local registration authority, registration authority and certificate authority, with the first link usually synchronous and the later ones synchronous or asynchronous. Communication may be over online connections, over asynchronous links, or offline through files.
sections.plainLanguage: The device always starts the conversation. It sends a signed request to a registration authority, which checks it and either answers or passes it on to the certificate authority. A registration authority can add its own signature to a message it forwards. The chain can be as short as a device talking straight to a certificate authority.

sections.title: The CMP Message Header
sections.content:
Every CMP message has the same outer structure: a header, a body, and optionally a protection field and an extraCerts field. The body carries the operation-specific information. The RFC specifies each header field exhaustively.

  • pvno is required and is 3 for CMP version 3 wherever EnvelopedData is supported and expected, and 3 in a certConf message that uses the hashAlg field; it is 2 in all other cases.
  • sender is required. For signature-based protection it must be the subject of the CMP protection certificate; for MAC-based protection it must carry a name the receiver can use to find the shared secret. In a multi-hop scenario the receiver cannot rely on it being correct.
  • recipient is required, and in the first message of an operation should be the subject of the certificate authority being asked. Later messages should carry the sender value of the previous message.
  • protectionAlg is required and names the algorithm used for the protection bits.
  • transactionID is required. In the first message of an operation it must be 128 bits of random data, to make a clash with an existing transaction unlikely; later messages repeat the same value.
  • senderNonce is required and must be 128 cryptographically secure random bits, fresh for each message. The recipNonce echoes the sender nonce of the previous message.
  • messageTime is optional but must be present when confirmWaitTime is present.
  • implicitConfirm asks the other side to skip the certificate confirmation message, and confirmWaitTime tells it how long it may wait. The two are mutually exclusive.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with the same header. It names the sender and the intended recipient, says which algorithm protects the message, carries a random transaction number so that replies can be matched to requests, and carries a fresh random number that the other side echoes back.

sections.title: Enrolling an End Entity to a New PKI
sections.content:
This operation asks a new PKI for a certificate, using a certificate from an external PKI, such as a manufacturer-issued device certificate, to authenticate itself. The end entity's certificate must have been enrolled by that external PKI, and the PKI management entity must hold the trust anchor of the external PKI.

The flow has two shapes. The end entity sends an initialization request, ir, which contains exactly one CertReqMsg. The management entity handles or forwards it and answers with an initialization response, ip. If the end entity asked for implicit confirmation and the management entity grants it, the exchange stops there. Otherwise the end entity sends a certificate confirmation, certConf, and the management entity answers with a PKI confirmation, pkiConf. If the expected confirmation does not arrive in time, the management entity must treat it as a rejection, and may then revoke the certificate, notify a monitoring system or log the event.

If the request was rejected, the response must carry the status code rejection and omit the certifiedKeyPair field, and the end entity must not send a confirmation.

The RFC spells out the fields of the request in full. The CertReqMsg must carry a certificate request identifier of 0, a certificate template whose subject holds the end entity's identity, and the public key to be certified. A proof-of-possession signature must be present when the key is generated locally, and must be absent when central key generation is requested. The algorithm identifier must match the public key algorithm, and the signature is computed over the DER-encoded request.
sections.plainLanguage: A device that already has a manufacturer certificate asks a new PKI for an operational certificate. It sends a request naming the identity and the public key it wants certified, and signs the request to prove it holds the matching private key. The server may reply straight away, or it may ask the device to confirm that it received and accepted the certificate, which takes one extra exchange.

sections.title: What the Registration Authority Does
sections.content:
Section 5 covers the behaviour of the PKI management entities. A registration authority can respond to a request itself, forward it upstream, or act on behalf of an end entity.

When responding to a certificate request, the authority produces the response message itself. When responding to a confirmation message, it produces the matching PKI confirmation. When forwarding, there are three options. It can forward without changing the protection, leaving the original end entity's signature intact. It can add its own protection and, where several requests need to go upstream together, batch them into a single nested message. Or it can replace the protection, replacing the end entity's proof-of-possession with one of its own, using the raVerified field to record that it has verified the original.

Acting on behalf of another entity means the registration authority takes the role of the end entity in the operations of Section 4, for example requesting a certificate on behalf of a device it serves, or revoking one.
sections.plainLanguage: A registration authority has three choices: answer the request itself, pass it on unchanged, or pass it on with its own signature added. It can also sign several requests together in one batched message, or take over the device's role and act on its behalf.

sections.title: How the Messages Travel
sections.content:
CMP messages are self-contained, so in principle any reliable transport can carry them. An end entity will typically support only one. PKI management entities should offer HTTP and may offer CoAP where it is needed. Piggybacking on another reliable protocol such as EAP or MQTT may be used, and file-based transfer may be used when offline transfer is required.

Whatever the transport, messages can be lost or a peer may not answer, so each entity that sends a request should use a configurable per-request timeout, and each management entity should use a configurable timeout when it expects a further request in the same transaction. A hanging transaction can then be closed with an error and its resources freed. Where a response is genuinely delayed, the CMP-level polling messages handle it; other delays are better handled at the transport level.

Over HTTP, the URI path must be /.well-known/cmp or /.well-known/cmp/p/<name>, followed by an operation label such as initialization, keyupdate, revocation or getcacerts. Over CoAP the same paths are used with shorter labels such as ir, cr and kur. The media type for HTTP, CoAP and MIME transfer must be application/pkixcmp. For file-based transfer, each file must hold exactly one ASN.1 DER encoded CMP message, with no extra header or trailer, and the filename extension must be .pki.

The RFC notes that the main security goal for certificate management is integrity and data origin authentication, and that confidentiality matters when centrally generated keys are delivered. CMP itself achieves these goals, including end to end. TLS can be used as a second line of defence for hop-by-hop confidentiality and privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages can travel over HTTP, over CoAP for small devices, over another reliable protocol, or as files on disk for offline use. Each message is self-contained, so a single exchange carries everything needed. Whatever the transport, the client sets a timeout so that a lost reply does not leave the exchange hanging.

sections.title: What Implementations Must Support
sections.content:
Section 7 states, for each operation, whether support is mandatory, recommended, optional or not applicable for an end entity, a registration authority and a certificate authority.

For an end entity, the mandatory set is small: the generic aspects of the messages and operations, enrolling to a new PKI, and updating a valid certificate. Revocation is recommended. Everything else, including enrolment to a known PKI, PKCS #10 based enrolment, MAC-based protection, central key generation, the support messages and polling, is optional for an end entity.

For a certificate authority, responding to a certificate request and to a confirmation message are mandatory, along with the generic requirements, enrolling to a new PKI and updating a certificate. For a registration authority, most operations are optional, and MAC-based protection is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: A device that conforms to this profile has to implement only three things: the common message rules, getting a first certificate, and renewing it. Everything else is optional. A certificate authority has to implement more, because it is the one that actually issues certificates.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of CMP, the CMP updates, the algorithm specification, CRMF, the algorithm requirements update, and the HTTP and CoAP transfer documents all apply.

Trust anchors for chain validation are often held as self-signed certificates. All trust anchors MUST be stored on the device with integrity protection. Where a device has too little storage for the complete certificates, it may store only a hash of each one and require the certificate to be sent in the extraCerts field of the messages; such certificates supplied in band must then be verified against the trust store.

For TLS that authenticates with shared secret information, a pre-shared key and a password-authenticated key exchange give the same protection against a real-time attack, which is the amount of entropy in the secret. They differ in long-term confidentiality: a pre-shared key cipher suite is only as secure as the entropy of the secret, while a password-authenticated key exchange remains secure even if the secret is weak.
sections.plainLanguage: The trust anchors a device relies on must be protected against tampering, and if the device has no room for them it can keep a hash and ask for the certificate each time. When TLS uses a shared password rather than certificates, a password-based key exchange is the safer choice, because it stays secure even when the password is weak.
